item.title: Running Kali Linux Containers on a Linux Server with Docker
item.description: Kali Linux ships official OCI images under kalilinux/kali-rolling, kalilinux/kali-last-release, and kalilinux/kali-bleeding-edge. They are deliberately minimal, containing little beyond the base userland, so tooling is layered on top through Kali’s metapackages. That makes them well suited to disposable, reproducible assessment environments on a remote server: you get a clean toolchain per engagement, isolated from the host and from each other, without maintaining a full Kali VM. Use them only against systems you are authorized to test.

item.title: Set up rootfs of a Debian VM with virtiofsd for Linux Kernel Testing
item.description: The expensive part of a kernel test loop is rarely the compile. Its the plumbing between a finished bzImage and a userspace that can exercise it: re-packing an initramfs, loopback-mounting a disk image to drop modules into it, or standing up an NFS server so the guest has somewhere to mount as root. virtiofs collapses all of that into a directory. The guest’s root filesystem is a plain directory tree on the host, exported by virtiofsd over a vhost-user socket and mounted by the guest kernel with root=<tag> rootfstype=virtiofs. There’s no image format, no partition table and no block layer, so the rootfs can be built with ordinary package-manager tooling, modified with ordinary host tools while the VM is running, and snapshotted with cp --reflink. This post builds a Debian 13 (trixie) rootfs with mmdebstrap, exports it with virtiofsd, boots it under QEMU with a locally built kernel, and arranges for modules, selftests and the kernel tree itself to appear in the guest without any image rebuild step. Debian is a good fit because its minimal bootstrap is small, its package set covers nearly every kernel-adjacent tool (linux-perf, bpftool, trace-cmd, stress-ng), and it is the userspace most existing kernel CI tooling, syzkaller included, already assumes.

item.title: Installing Linux on External SSD
item.description: I wanted to install Linux on a portable SSD and make it bootable from my laptop, it required UEFI support. I came up with my own method since I couldn’t find a better way to do it online.
